subtopics.title: Classification of force systems
subtopics.theory_md:
Forces are classified by where their lines of action lie.
- **Coplanar**: all in one plane. **Non-coplanar** (space): not in one plane.
- Within each: **collinear** (one common line), **concurrent** (meet at a point), **parallel** (like = same sense, unlike = opposite), **non-concurrent non-parallel** (general).

Examples: forces at a truss joint are coplanar concurrent; loads and reactions on a beam are coplanar parallel; a plane truss with its loads and reactions is coplanar non-concurrent; a tripod's legs are non-coplanar concurrent.

Independent equations: coplanar concurrent 2 ($\sum F_x,\sum F_y$); coplanar general 3 (add $\sum M$); space concurrent 3; space general 6.
subtopics.basics_md: A force system is just a group of forces on one body. We sort the group by two questions: do the lines lie in one flat plane, and do they cross at one point? The answers decide which equations of equilibrium you may use.
key_points: Coplanar: lines of action in one plane; non-coplanar: not in one plane
Collinear, concurrent, parallel (like or unlike), non-concurrent non-parallel
Truss joint = coplanar concurrent; beam under vertical loads = coplanar parallel; plane truss with loads and reactions = coplanar non-concurrent
Coplanar concurrent needs 2 equations, coplanar general needs 3

questions.q: Name the types of coplanar force systems and give one engineering example of each.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Coplanar force systems** (all lines of action in one plane):
1. **Collinear**: all along one line, e.g. forces in a rope in a tug of war.
2. **Concurrent**: lines meet at a point, e.g. member forces at a truss joint.
3. **Parallel** (like or unlike): e.g. vertical loads and reactions on a simply supported beam.
4. **Non-concurrent non-parallel** (general): e.g. the loads and reactions on a plane truss.

points: Coplanar: collinear, concurrent, parallel (like/unlike), non-concurrent non-parallel, each with an example
Non-coplanar: concurrent, parallel, non-concurrent non-parallel, with examples (tripod, table legs, crane)
Coplanar non-concurrent: lines of action in one plane but not meeting at a point
Causes translation and rotation; needs $\sum F_x=0$, $\sum F_y=0$, $\sum M=0$
Examples: simply supported beam with loads and reactions, ladder against a wall, plane truss

subtopics.title: Perfect, deficient and redundant frames
subtopics.theory_md:
A **frame** (truss) is a pin-jointed assembly of members. With $m$ members and $j$ joints:
- **Perfect frame**: $m=2j-3$. Just enough members to keep its shape; statically determinate. Example: triangle ($j=3,m=3$).
- **Imperfect frame**: $m\neq 2j-3$.
  - **Deficient**: $m<2j-3$, too few members, unstable, collapses like a mechanism (square of 4 bars: $4<5$).
  - **Redundant**: $m>2j-3$, extra members, statically indeterminate (square with both diagonals: $6>5$).

Check with supports: $m+r=2j$ with $r=3$ reaction components (one hinge + one roller).
subtopics.basics_md: A triangle cannot change shape without changing a side, so it is rigid. Each new joint added with two new members keeps it rigid, which is why every new joint adds 2 members: $m=3+2(j-3)=2j-3$.
key_points: Perfect frame: $m=2j-3$, rigid and statically determinate
Imperfect frame: $m\neq 2j-3$, either deficient or redundant
Deficient: $m<2j-3$, unstable, collapses under load
Redundant: $m>2j-3$, stable but statically indeterminate
Examples: triangle (perfect), square of 4 bars (deficient), square with 2 diagonals (redundant)

questions.q: Classify the following plane frames as perfect, deficient or redundant: (a) $j=6$, $m=8$; (b) $j=8$, $m=13$; (c) $j=7$, $m=12$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Use $2j-3$:
(a) $2(6)-3=9$; $m=8<9$, so **deficient** (one member short).
(b) $2(8)-3=13$; $m=13$, so **perfect**.
(c) $2(7)-3=11$; $m=12>11$, so **redundant** (one extra member).

questions.q: A truss has 9 joints and 14 members. It is supported on a hinge and a roller. Is it stable and determinate? How many members must be added or removed?
questions.model_answer_md: $2j-3=2(9)-3=15$. Here $m=14<15$, so the frame is **deficient** by one member. With $r=3$ reactions, $m+r=17<2j=18$, so there are fewer unknowns than equations: it is a mechanism, not determinate. **Add one member** (suitably placed) to make it perfect.

points: Deficient: $m<2j-3$, fewer members than needed, unstable, changes shape under load
Redundant: $m>2j-3$, more members than needed, stable but statically indeterminate

subtopics.title: Types of trusses and assumptions
subtopics.theory_md:
A **truss** is a perfect frame of straight members joined at pins to carry loads at joints.

**Assumptions**: (1) the frame is perfect, $m=2j-3$; (2) joints are frictionless pins; (3) loads act only at joints; (4) members are straight and carry only axial force, tension or compression; (5) self-weight is neglected.

**Types**: *Pratt* (diagonals slope down to the centre, in tension); *Howe* (opposite, diagonals in compression); *Warren* (equilateral triangles, no verticals); *K-truss*; *Fink* and *king-post / queen-post* (roofs); *north-light* (factory roofs). **Plane** truss: all members in one plane; **space** truss: 3-D.

A **determinate** structure: reactions and member forces follow from statics alone.
subtopics.basics_md: Every member of an ideal truss has a pin at each end and no load in between, so it can only be pulled or pushed along its own length. That is why we can solve each joint by two force equations alone.
key_points: Assumptions: perfect frame, frictionless pins, loads at joints only, axial force only, negligible self-weight
Pratt: diagonals in tension; Howe: diagonals in compression; Warren: equilateral triangles
Roof trusses: Fink, king-post, queen-post, north-light
Determinate: found from $\sum F_x=0,\sum F_y=0,\sum M=0$ alone; indeterminate if unknowns exceed equations

questions.q: State the assumptions made in the analysis of a perfect truss. Why must loads be applied at the joints?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Assumptions**
1. The frame is **perfect**, $m=2j-3$.
2. Joints are **frictionless pins**, so no moment is transmitted.
3. Loads and reactions act **only at joints**.
4. Members are straight and carry only **axial force** (tension or compression).
5. **Self-weight** is neglected.

A load between joints would bend the member, so it would no longer be a two-force axial member.

subtopics.title: Resultant of concurrent forces and moment of a force
subtopics.theory_md:
Resolve each force into components, add, recombine:
$$\sum F_x=\sum F_i\cos\theta_i,\quad \sum F_y=\sum F_i\sin\theta_i$$
$$R=\sqrt{(\sum F_x)^2+(\sum F_y)^2},\quad \tan\alpha=\frac{\sum F_y}{\sum F_x}$$
($\theta$ from the $+x$ axis anticlockwise; fix the quadrant from the signs.) Two forces: parallelogram law, $R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$.

**Moment** of a force about a point $=F\times d$ ($d$ perpendicular distance), anticlockwise positive. **Varignon**: the moment of the resultant about a point equals the sum of the moments of the components.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of pulling a ring with several strings. Each pull has a left-right part and an up-down part. Add the left-right parts together and the up-down parts together, and you get one single pull that does the same job.
key_points: Resultant from $\sum F_x$ and $\sum F_y$: $R=\sqrt{\sum F_x^2+\sum F_y^2}$
Direction $\tan\alpha=\sum F_y/\sum F_x$, check the quadrant from signs
Moment = force times perpendicular distance, with sign
Varignon: moment of resultant = sum of moments of components

questions.q: Three forces act at a point: 100 N along $0^\circ$, 150 N at $60^\circ$ and 200 N at $135^\circ$ (all measured anticlockwise from the $+x$ axis). Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
State Varignon's theorem and use it to find the moment about O of a 50 N force acting at point (3 m, 4 m) in direction $+x$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Varignon's theorem**: the moment of a force about a point equals the algebraic sum of the moments of its components about that point.

The force is $+50$ N in $x$ at $y=4$ m. Its line of action is 4 m above O, so $M_O=-50\times4=-200$ N·m (clockwise, 200 N·m).

subtopics.title: Couple and resultant of a force system
subtopics.theory_md:
A **couple** is two equal, opposite, parallel forces: moment $M=F\times d$ ($d$ between the lines), same about every point; it causes rotation only.

A force $F$ at a point can be moved to a point O if a couple $F\times d$ is added (**force-couple system**).

**Resultant of parallel forces**: $R=\sum F$ and its position from a reference point, $\bar x=\dfrac{\sum F x}{\sum F}$ (Varignon).

**Equilibrium** of a coplanar system: $\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0,\ \sum M=0$.
subtopics.basics_md: A couple is the twist you apply to a steering wheel: two hands, equal and opposite pushes. It turns the wheel but does not push the car sideways.
key_points: Couple: equal opposite parallel forces, $M=Fd$, free vector (same about every point)
A force moved parallel to itself needs a couple of moment $F\times d$
Resultant of parallel forces $R=\sum F$, position $\bar x=\sum Fx/\sum F$
Equilibrium: $\sum F_x=\sum F_y=\sum M=0$

questions.model_answer_md:

Moments about the left end: $R\bar x=10(0)+20(2)+15(5)=115$ kN·m

questions.q: Replace a 20 N vertical force acting 3 m to the right of point O by an equivalent force-couple system at O.
questions.model_answer_md:
Move the 20 N force to O (parallel to itself): a **20 N force at O**.
Add the couple that makes up the moment of the original force about O: $M=20\times3=60$ N·m (clockwise for a downward force on the right).
So the system is 20 N plus a couple of 60 N·m.

subtopics.title: Support reactions of a truss
subtopics.theory_md:
Always find the reactions first, from the whole truss as a free body.
- **Hinge** (pin): two components, $H$ and $V$.
- **Roller**: one component, perpendicular to the surface it rolls on.
- Equations: $\sum F_x=0$, $\sum F_y=0$, $\sum M=0$ (about a support, to eliminate two unknowns). For a perfect truss, $r=3$.

Resolve inclined loads into $x$ and $y$ components first; a load normal to a rafter makes angle $\theta$ with the vertical, giving $P\sin\theta$ and $P\cos\theta$. Check with a second moment equation.
subtopics.basics_md: The truss is one rigid body held by its supports. Three unknown reactions need three equations. Taking moments about the hinge removes both hinge components at once, leaving only the roller reaction.
key_points: Hinge: 2 reactions (H and V); roller: 1 reaction, perpendicular to the rolling surface
Take moments about the hinge to get the roller reaction directly
Resolve inclined loads into components first
Check $\sum F_y=0$ at the end

subtopics.title: Procedure, assumptions and limitations
subtopics.theory_md:
Isolate each joint as a free body: the member forces and the load at that joint are a **concurrent** system, so only $\sum F_x=0$ and $\sum F_y=0$ apply, giving **at most 2 unknowns per joint**.

**Steps**: (1) find the reactions; (2) start at a joint with only 2 unknown members (usually a support); (3) assume every unknown as **tension** (arrow away from the joint); (4) solve, then carry each found force to the next joint (a member's force acts in opposite sense at its two ends); (5) tabulate: $+$ is tension, $-$ is compression; (6) check with a last joint.

**Limitations**: needs a joint with 2 unknowns; errors carry forward; long for large trusses.
subtopics.basics_md: A pin in equilibrium has forces through one point only, so there is no moment equation. Two force equations can solve two unknown members. Walk from joint to joint, each time using the member force you just found.
key_points: Joint forces are concurrent, so only $\sum F_x=0$ and $\sum F_y=0$: at most 2 unknowns per joint
Find reactions first, start at a joint with 2 unknowns
Assume tension (away from the joint); positive result tension, negative compression
Assumptions: perfect frame, pins, joint loads, axial forces, no self-weight
Limitations: errors carry forward, long for big trusses

questions.q: List the steps of the method of joints.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Find the **support reactions** from the equilibrium of the whole truss.
2. Choose a joint with **at most two unknown members** (usually a support joint).
3. Draw its free body; assume unknown forces as **tension** (away from the joint) and resolve inclined ones.
4. Apply $\sum F_x=0$ and $\sum F_y=0$ and solve.
5. Move to the next joint using the forces already found (opposite sense at the other end).
6. Tabulate with $+$ for tension and $-$ for compression; check the last joint.

subtopics.title: Zero-force members and special joints
subtopics.theory_md:
At an **unloaded** joint (no external load or reaction):
1. **Two members**, not in line: both carry **zero** force.
2. **Three members, two collinear**: the third (not in line) carries **zero** force; the two collinear members carry equal force.
3. **Two members in line, load along the same line**: the force passes through unchanged.

If a load or reaction acts along one member, that member balances it and the other (non-collinear) member is zero.

Removing zero-force members first shortens the work. They stay useful for stability and for other loadings.
subtopics.basics_md: If only two bars meet at a pin and they point in different directions, nothing can balance a push in one bar, since the other bar cannot push back sideways. So both must carry nothing.
key_points: Unloaded joint with two non-collinear members: both zero
Unloaded joint with three members, two collinear: the third is zero
Collinear members carry equal force
Zero-force members still needed for stability or other loads

questions.q: State the two rules used to identify zero-force members in a truss. Why are such members provided?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Rule 1**: if two non-collinear members meet at an unloaded joint, both carry zero force.
**Rule 2**: if three members meet at an unloaded joint and two are collinear, the third carries zero force.

Zero-force members are provided for **stability** (to keep the truss perfect and prevent buckling of long members) and to carry load when the loading changes.

questions.q: In the truss ACE with bottom chord A-B-C and vertical BD up to D, a load acts only at D. Joint B has members AB, BC and BD (AB and BC are collinear); B has no load or support. Find the force in BD and the relation between AB and BC.
questions.model_answer_md:
Joint B is unloaded with three members, AB and BC collinear. By Rule 2: $F_{BD}=0$ (vertical, nothing to balance it).
Then $\sum F_x=0$ at B gives $F_{AB}=F_{BC}$: the two bottom-chord members carry the same force and nature.
points: $F_{BD}=0$ by rule for three members, two collinear

subtopics.title: Method of joints: standard numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
A usual numerical: perfect truss, vertical loads, hinge and roller.
1. Reactions: $\sum M_A=0$ for the roller, then $\sum F_y=0$.
2. Start at a support joint (2 unknowns); angles of $60^\circ$ (equilateral) give $\sin60^\circ=0.866$, $\cos60^\circ=0.5$.
3. Move along; use symmetry and zero-force rules to skip work.
4. Tabulate member, magnitude, nature (T or C).

At each joint: $\sum F_y=0$ first for the inclined member, then $\sum F_x=0$ for the horizontal one. A load at the support joint goes straight into the equations. If a joint becomes the third with unknowns, go back to another joint.
subtopics.basics_md: You are solving a chain of small problems, each two equations in two unknowns. Starting at a support is easiest because only two members meet there. Keep a table of what you have found.

subtopics.title: Method of joints: inclined, horizontal and special loads
subtopics.theory_md:
Same method with three extra steps.
1. **Resolve each inclined load** into $x$ and $y$ components before using it in the reactions or at its joint. A load normal to a rafter at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal has components $P\sin\theta$ (horizontal) and $P\cos\theta$ (vertical).
2. **Horizontal loads** give a horizontal hinge reaction and a moment about the hinge (arm = height).
3. **Special supports** (roller on a wall, cable): the roller reaction is perpendicular to its surface.

Use the zero-force rules and symmetry. If a load acts along the line of a member, joint equations along and normal to the member are easier than $x$-$y$. Always finish with a check joint.
subtopics.basics_md: Nothing new in principle: reactions first, then joints. The extra work is resolving the slanted loads into straight components, and remembering that a horizontal load pushes the whole truss sideways, so the hinge must push back.
key_points: Resolve inclined loads into components first

subtopics.title: Principle and procedure
subtopics.theory_md:
Cut the truss by an imaginary section through **not more than three members** whose forces are unknown (and not all meeting at one point). Either part is a free body in equilibrium under the loads, reactions and the cut-member forces:
$$\sum F_x=0,\quad \sum F_y=0,\quad \sum M=0$$

**Steps**: (1) find reactions; (2) pass section 1-1 through the required members; (3) assume cut forces as **tension** (away from the cut); (4) take moments about the point where two unknown forces meet, which gives the third directly; (5) negative = compression.

| | Joints | Sections |
|---|---|---|
| Free body | one joint, concurrent | a part, non-concurrent |
| Equations | 2 | 3 |
| Unknowns | 2 | 3 |
| Best for | all members | a few chosen members |
subtopics.basics_md: If you cut a loaf of bread, the slice you hold must still be in balance. The knife-cut forces are the unknown member forces. Choose the cut so that only three unknowns appear, then three equations are enough.
key_points: Section passes through at most 3 unknown members, not concurrent
Apply $\sum F_x=\sum F_y=\sum M=0$ on one part
Moments about the intersection of two unknowns give the third directly
Assume tension; negative answer means compression
Joints: all members; sections: selected members, no error carried forward

subtopics.title: Method of sections: numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
**Choosing the moment centre.**
- Chord member: moments about the joint where the other two cut members meet, or the point on the opposite chord.
- Diagonal: usually $\sum F_y=0$ on the cut part; otherwise moments about the point where the two chords meet when extended.
- Parallel chords: $\sum F_y=0$ for the diagonal.

Resolve an inclined member at the joint it passes through, with its horizontal and vertical components times their lever arms. If the section leaves a part with no support reaction (like the top of a tower), use that part so reactions are not needed.

Use the zero-force rule first if a joint is unloaded.
subtopics.basics_md: A numerical is: reactions, draw the section, pick the part with fewer forces, write moments about the clever points. Each member needs one equation if you choose the points well.

subtopics.title: Tension coefficient and joint equations
subtopics.theory_md:
The **tension coefficient** of a member of length $L$ and tension $T$ is
$$t=\frac{T}{L}\quad(\text{force per unit length};\ t>0\ \text{tension},\ t<0\ \text{compression})$$

For a member from joint 1 $(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ to joint 2, its pull on joint 1 has components
$$X=t(x_2-x_1),\quad Y=t(y_2-y_1),\quad Z=t(z_2-z_1)$$
So no angles are needed, only coordinates.

**At each joint**: $\sum t\,\Delta x+P_x=0,\ \sum t\,\Delta y+P_y=0,\ \sum t\,\Delta z+P_z=0$. Solve for $t$'s, then $T=tL$, with $L=\sqrt{\Delta x^2+\Delta y^2+\Delta z^2}$.

Mainly used for **space trusses** (3 equations per joint, so up to 3 unknowns).
subtopics.basics_md: Instead of finding angles and sines, we scale the force by the member length. Then each force component is just the coordinate difference times t. The equations look the same for every joint, which is why it suits computers and 3-D trusses.
key_points: Tension coefficient $t=T/L$: positive tension, negative compression
Force components on a joint: $t\Delta x,\ t\Delta y,\ t\Delta z$
Joint equilibrium: $\sum t\Delta x+P_x=0$ etc.
Member force $T=tL$ with $L$ from coordinates
Space truss: 3 equations per joint

questions.q: Derive the components of a member force in terms of its tension coefficient.
questions.model_answer_md:
Let a member of length $L$ run from joint 1 to joint 2 with tension $T$. Its direction cosines are $(x_2-x_1)/L$ etc., so the pull on joint 1 along the member has components
$X=T\dfrac{x_2-x_1}{L}=t(x_2-x_1)$, $Y=t(y_2-y_1)$, $Z=t(z_2-z_1)$ where $t=T/L$.
The force on joint 2 is equal and opposite.

subtopics.title: Tension coefficients: plane and space numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
**Plane joint** (2 equations): write $\sum t\Delta x+P_x=0$ and $\sum t\Delta y+P_y=0$ using coordinates of the other ends, then $T=tL$.

**Space joint**: with 3 members meeting at a loaded joint, solve the three equations for the three $t$'s.

Take $\Delta$ as (far end minus the joint under study). Include external load components with their sign; a downward load is $-P$ in $z$ or $y$.

**Worked plane example**: load 10 kN down at O(0,0); members to A(-3,4) and B(3,4). $-3t_A+3t_B=0$ and $4t_A+4t_B-10=0$, so $t_A=t_B=1.25$ and $T=1.25\times5=6.25$ kN each (tension).
subtopics.basics_md: Write the joint equations, plug in the coordinate differences, solve like simultaneous equations, then multiply by length. The only trap is the sign of the load and the order of subtracting coordinates.
key_points: Set up $\sum t\Delta x+P_x=0$ and the $y$, $z$ equations at the joint
$\Delta$ = far end minus joint; include load with sign
$T=tL$ for the magnitude and nature
Symmetry reduces unknowns in a tripod

questions.q: A joint O at the origin has a member to A(4, 3). Length $L$ of the member is
A load of 10 kN hangs downward from joint O at the origin, supported by two members OA and OB going up to A(-3, 4) m and B(3, 4) m. Using tension coefficients, find the forces in OA and OB.
questions.model_answer_md:
Equilibrium of joint O (coordinates of A and B relative to O):
$\sum X=0$: $t_{OA}(-3)+t_{OB}(3)=0\Rightarrow t_{OA}=t_{OB}=t$
$\sum Y=0$: $t_{OA}(4)+t_{OB}(4)-10=0\Rightarrow 8t=10\Rightarrow t=1.25$ kN/m
$L=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ m, so $T_{OA}=T_{OB}=1.25\times5=6.25$ kN (tension).

questions.q: A tripod has its apex O at the origin and its feet at A(2, 0, -4), B(-1, 1.732, -4) and C(-1, -1.732, -4) m (z upward). A vertical load of 30 kN acts downward at O. Find the force in each leg.
questions.model_answer_md:
By symmetry $t_{OA}=t_{OB}=t_{OC}=t$.
$\sum Z=0$: $t(-4)+t(-4)+t(-4)-30=0\Rightarrow t=-2.5$ kN/m
$\sum X=0$: $t(2-1-1)=0$ is satisfied; $\sum Y=0$: $t(1.732-1.732)=0$ is satisfied.
Length of each leg $L=\sqrt{2^2+4^2}=\sqrt{20}=4.472$ m (check B: $1+3+16=20$).
$T=tL=-2.5\times4.472=-11.18$ kN, so **each leg carries 11.18 kN in compression**.

subtopics.title: Force polygon and funicular polygon
subtopics.theory_md:
**Force polygon**: draw the forces to scale, head to tail in order. The closing line (start to end) is the **resultant** in magnitude and direction. If it closes, the resultant force is zero. (Law of polygon of forces.)

**Funicular (link) polygon**: for non-concurrent forces. On the space diagram, draw links parallel to the rays joining a pole O to the vertices of the force polygon. The first and last links, extended, meet on the line of action of the resultant, which fixes its **position**.

**Equilibrium**: force polygon closes (no resultant force) and funicular polygon closes (no resultant couple).

Use: resultant of non-concurrent forces and **reactions of a beam** (closing line of the funicular polygon). **Bow's notation** letters the spaces; a force is named by the spaces on its two sides.
subtopics.basics_md: The force polygon tells you how big the resultant is and which way it points. The funicular polygon, drawn like a hanging rope, tells you where it sits. You need both to replace a set of loads by a single equivalent force.
key_points: Force polygon: forces head to tail, closing line is the resultant in magnitude and direction
Funicular polygon: links parallel to the rays from a pole; fixes the line of action of the resultant
Closed force polygon: no resultant force; closed funicular: no couple
Bow's notation: name forces by the spaces on both sides
Used for resultant of non-concurrent forces and reactions of beams

subtopics.title: Graphical analysis of a truss
subtopics.theory_md:
The **stress (Maxwell-Bow) diagram** gives all member forces of a truss in one drawing.
1. Draw the truss to scale; letter the **spaces** (Bow's notation); each member is named by the two spaces on its sides.
2. Find the reactions (analytically or by the funicular polygon).
3. Draw the external force polygon (loads and reactions) in order, going clockwise round the truss.
4. Start at a joint with two unknown members: draw the force polygon of that joint (closed), lines parallel to the members.
5. Move joint to joint; each new member adds a point to the diagram.
6. **Nature**: transfer the arrow from the diagram to the joint. Arrow **towards** the joint is compression, **away** from the joint is tension. Magnitude by the scale.
subtopics.basics_md: Every joint is a closed polygon of forces. Bow's notation draws all of them in one picture so that each member force appears once as a single line, to scale.
key_points: Letter spaces by Bow's notation; member named by the two spaces beside it
Reactions first; external force polygon drawn clockwise
Each joint is a closed force polygon: start where two unknowns remain
Arrow towards the joint: compression; away from the joint: tension
Member forces read off to scale

questions.q: The apex joint of a symmetrical truss carries a 20 kN vertical load and two members each inclined at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal meet there. Find the force in each member using the force triangle (sine rule).
questions.model_answer_md:
Each member pushes up on the joint along a line at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. The closed force triangle (the 20 kN load and the two member forces) is isosceles with base angles $30^\circ$ and apex angle $120^\circ$.
Sine rule: $\dfrac{F}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{20}{\sin120^\circ}\Rightarrow F=\dfrac{20(0.5)}{0.866}=11.55$ kN.
The arrows point towards the joint, so both members are in **compression**, 11.55 kN each.
points: Closed force triangle at the joint

questions.q: Describe the steps of the graphical method of finding member forces of a truss and how the nature of each force is decided.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Draw the truss to scale and letter the spaces by **Bow's notation**.
2. Find the **reactions** and draw the external force polygon clockwise.
3. Begin at a joint with **two unknowns**; draw its closed polygon with lines parallel to the members.
4. Proceed joint to joint until all members are drawn.
5. Measure the lengths to scale for the magnitudes.
6. **Nature**: transfer the arrow to the joint: towards the joint is compression, away from the joint is tension.
